logs.tagline: A log summariser for the command line
logs.desc: {brand} reads plain text log files and prints a short summary of what is in them.
logs.overview: {brand} reads plain text log files and prints a short summary: how many lines there are, which levels they use and which messages repeat the most. It is one small binary with no dependencies.
features: Reads files, directories and standard input
Groups similar messages without any configuration
Prints text, JSON or a small HTML report
logs.quick_out:
app.log: 48 211 lines, 3 levels
  info   46 902
  warn    1 190
  error     119
top message: cache miss for key (9 413 times)
logs.install_intro: {brand} is distributed as a single binary. There is nothing to configure before the first run.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the binary to a directory on your PATH.
Run the version command to check that it works.

faq.a: Anything line based. {brand} recognises common timestamp and level styles and falls back to plain lines when it does not.

faq.q: How big a file can it read?
faq.a: Files are streamed, so size is limited only by time. A gigabyte takes a few seconds on a laptop.

usage.p: Point {brand} at a file, a directory or a pipe. Directories are read recursively and compressed files are unpacked on the fly.
Use --since and --until to narrow the summary to a time range. Times can be absolute or relative to now.
The default output is plain text. JSON is stable and meant for scripts; the HTML report is a single file you can send to a colleague.

options.d: Only lines after this time, absolute or such as 2h.
Only lines before this time.
Only lines of this level or above.
How many repeated messages to list. Default 5.
text, json or html. Default text.

logs.config_intro: {brand} reads an optional file called config.toml in your configuration folder. Every key can also be given on the command line, and the command line wins.

config_rows.d: How many repeated messages to list.
The output format: text, json or html.
Messages to leave out, matched as plain text.
Only read lines after this time.

recipes.p: Group the summary by hour to see when the log was busiest.
Show which messages are new, and which went away, between two files.

recipes.h: Make a report to send round
recipes.p: Write the HTML report to a file and attach it to a message.

trouble.a: Check that the file has one message per line. If it is compressed in a format {brand} does not know, unpack it first.
Lines without a time zone are read as UTC. Use --tz to say which zone they are in.
Lower --top, or add the noisiest messages to the ignore list in the configuration file.

trouble.q: It is slow on a network drive
trouble.a: Copy the file to a local disk first. Reading line by line over a slow link is the usual cause.

site.desc: {brand} turns a folder of Markdown files and a few templates into a static website.
site.overview: {brand} turns a folder of Markdown files and a few templates into a static website. There is no database, no runtime and nothing to keep up to date on the server.
features: A local preview that rebuilds on every save
site.quick_out: Serving notes at localhost:4000 (press Ctrl+C to stop)
site.install_intro: {brand} is a single executable. Put it on your PATH and you are done.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the executable to a directory on your PATH.
Run the version command to check that it works.

faq.q: Can I use my own templates?
faq.a: Yes. Templates are plain HTML files with a few placeholders, and the folder layout is yours to change.
No. The output is plain files that any web server can serve.

faq.q: How do I add a new kind of page?
faq.a: Add a folder under pages with its own layout file and {brand} will pick it up on the next build.

usage.p: The init command creates a folder with a config file, a layout and one example page.
Pages are Markdown files. The front matter at the top sets the title and the date; everything below it is the content.
The build command writes the finished site to the public folder. Copy that folder to any web server.

options.d: Folder for the finished site. Default public.
Include pages marked as drafts.
Port for the preview server. Default 4000.
Rebuild when a file changes.
Print errors only.

site.config_intro: The file site.toml sits in the root of your folder. A missing key falls back to its default, so a new site needs no file at all.

config_rows.d: The name shown in the page header and in the title.
The address your site lives at. Use / for a site at the root.
The look of the site: plain, slate or folio.
Whether pages marked as drafts are built.

recipes.p: Create a Markdown file with a title and a date at the top.
Serve the site locally with the unfinished pages included.
Build the whole site into one folder that you can copy to any web server.

trouble.q: A page is missing from the build
trouble.a: Pages with draft: true in their header are skipped. Remove it or build with --drafts.
Set base_url to the address of the folder the site is published in.
Some editors write a new file instead of changing the old one. Restart the preview, or turn off safe write in the editor.
Put them in the static folder. Everything in it is copied unchanged.

jobs.desc: {brand} runs small recurring jobs on one machine and tells you when one of them fails.
jobs.overview: {brand} runs small recurring jobs on one machine and tells you when one of them fails. It is a friendlier alternative to a crontab you have to keep in your head.
features: One line of output per job, so failures stand out
jobs.quick_out: backup   every day at 03:00   last run: ok (4 s)
jobs.install_intro: {brand} is a single executable plus a small background process that checks the schedule once a minute.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the executable to a directory on your PATH.
Start the background process with your system's service manager.

faq.q: Does it need to run as a service?
faq.a: Yes, a small background process checks the schedule once a minute. The install page shows what to start.

faq.q: What happens if the computer is off?
faq.a: A job that was due while the machine was off runs once when it starts again.

faq.q: Can jobs depend on each other?
faq.a: Not yet. Chain the commands in a single job for now.

usage.p: A job has a name, a schedule and a command. Schedules are written in plain words.
The list command shows every job with the result of its last run. The history command shows the runs of one job with their duration and output.
Pausing keeps the job and its history but stops it from running. Useful while you move house or restore a backup.

options.d: Where jobs and logs are kept. Default is a folder in your home.
Print only failures.
How many runs history shows. Default 10.
Machine readable output.
Run a job right away as well as on schedule.

jobs.config_intro: {brand} reads jobs.toml from your configuration folder. The jobs themselves are kept separately, so the file only holds settings.

config_rows.d: The shell that runs the commands.
Where the output of every run is kept.
How many times a failed job is tried again.
Whether a failed job also sends a notice.

recipes.p: Start a job outside its schedule, for instance to test a new command.
Print the output of the last run of a job.
Stop all schedules until you resume them.

trouble.a: Check that the program is running with the list command. Jobs only run while it is.
Two copies of the program are running. Stop one of them; the lock file is in the log folder.

trouble.q: The command works in my shell but not here
trouble.a: Jobs do not read your shell startup files. Use full paths, or set the environment in the job.
{brand} follows the system clock and time zone. Change them there, not in the job.

csv.tagline: Select, sort and join CSV files
csv.desc: {brand} selects, sorts, joins and cleans CSV files from the command line.
csv.overview: {brand} selects, sorts, joins and cleans CSV files from the command line. It handles large files without loading them into memory and never changes the input.
features: Fix common problems such as stray quotes and mixed line endings
csv.install_intro: {brand} is a single executable with no dependencies.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the executable to a directory on your PATH.
Run the version command to check that it works.

faq.q: How large a file can it handle?
faq.a: Files are processed as a stream, so memory use stays small. Sorting large files uses temporary space on disk.
No. Output goes to the screen or to a new file.
Use the delimiter option for tabs, semicolons or any single character.

usage.p: The select command prints only the columns you name, in the order you give them. A column can be renamed with an equals sign.
The filter command keeps the rows that match a simple condition. Several conditions can be combined.
The join command combines two files on a column they share. Rows without a match are dropped unless you ask for them.

options.d: Field separator. Default is a comma.
Set to false if the first row is data.
Write to a file instead of the screen.
Column to sort by.
Column to join on.

csv.config_intro: Put a file called .{cmd}rc in your home folder to change the defaults. Options on the command line always win.

config_rows.d: Whether the first row holds column names.
The text encoding of input and output.
What an empty cell is written as in the output.

recipes.p: Keep two columns and give one of them a new name.

recipes.h: Join two files on a key
recipes.p: Combine the rows of two files that share an id.
Keep the first of every group of identical rows.

trouble.a: The file is probably not UTF-8. Set the encoding in the configuration file or with --encoding.
If the first row is data and not names, run with --no-header and refer to columns by number.
Say so with --numeric, or {brand} sorts them the way they look.
The key has different spacing or case in the two files. Run tidy on both and try again.
